# Surface and Geometry Alignment
## Overview
This family of methods addresses the fundamental limitation of vanilla 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS): the production of "floating" volumetric ellipsoids that lack an explicit, watertight geometric boundary [G]. By aligning the discrete Gaussian representation with continuous geometric priors (such as SDFs, depth maps, or explicit meshes), these methods enforce positional and normal consistency to enable accurate mesh extraction, physically-based rendering, and robust initialization [G]. Unlike sibling methods that may rely solely on photometric loss or implicit constraints, this family explicitly integrates geometric supervision into the training or post-processing pipeline to ensure the Gaussians conform to physical surfaces [G].
## Shared principles
See [Geometry and Surface Priors](9270-geometry-and-surface-priors.md) for the shared mechanism, terms, and math [G].
## Subtopics
[SuGaR](9191-sugar.md) is a post-hoc surface alignment method that converts the discrete 3DGS representation into a continuous, watertight triangle mesh via self-regularization and Poisson reconstruction. It differs from siblings by operating after initial training rather than during, solving the "floating" ellipsoid problem for downstream mesh applications like animation or physics. Choose it when explicit mesh extraction is required without modifying the training pipeline.

[Surface-guided Gaussian Re-initialization](9199-surface-guided-gaussian-re-initialization.md) is a training optimization that re-projects Gaussians onto a canonical surface mesh to resolve unbalanced aggregation caused by densification and splitting operations. It differs from siblings by explicitly repositioning Gaussians to a known geometry rather than relying on loss-driven alignment. Choose it when Gaussian distribution is uneven or clustered excessively during training.

[Geo-Splatting](9201-geo-splatting.md) is a physically-based inverse rendering method that differentiably constructs surface-aligned Gaussians from an explicit mesh to improve normal estimation and light transport modeling. It differs from siblings by using BVH-accelerated ray tracing on the mesh for accurate PBR, avoiding the approximated normals and semi-transparent nature of standard Gaussian points. Choose it when accurate material decomposition, relighting, or self-occlusion modeling is required.

[GeoCE Loss](17334-geoce-loss.md) is a geometric contrastive embedding method that aligns token similarity with 3D proximity to ensure clustering by physical surface rather than viewpoint. It differs from siblings by using soft contrastive targets derived from unprojected depths to shape the latent space, rather than enforcing hard positional or normal constraints. Choose it when feature-space similarity needs to be regularized by explicit 3D geometric consistency.
## Background
The concept of aligning Gaussian representations with geometric priors emerged as a solution to the lack of explicit geometry in 3D Gaussian Splatting [G]. While 3DGS excels at novel view synthesis, its volumetric nature makes mesh extraction difficult [G]. Early works like [SuGaR](9191-sugar.md) introduced post-hoc regularization to flatten Gaussians into surfels [G]. Subsequent methods like [Geo-Splatting](9201-geo-splatting.md) integrated explicit meshes for physically-based rendering, while others like [GeoCE Loss](17334-geoce-loss.md) focused on feature-space geometric consistency [G]. The family continues to evolve with methods addressing initialization and sparse-view constraints [G].
